summary: Pfizer Inc.’s Form 10-K is its annual report for the year ended December 31, 2022, filed with the SEC. It identifies the company, its securities, offices, filing status, filer classification, internal-control attestation, market value and shares outstanding, and proxy materials incorporated by reference. The contents list disclosures on Pfizer’s business, operations, products, research, risks, properties, legal matters and officers; equity, management analysis, market risks, financial statements and controls; governance, compensation, ownership and related parties; and exhibits, financial schedules, summary and signatures.

nodes.summary: Defines Pfizer-related terms, fiscal year conventions and the extensive abbreviations, entities, products, markets, accounting concepts, laws and medical terms used in its 2022 Form 10-K. Notes that clinical-study discussions require broader-data context and regulatory authorities may disagree; figures may differ due to rounding, percentages use unrounded amounts, and trademarks belong to their owners. Explains FDA emergency-use limitations for Paxlovid and COVID-19 vaccines. Describes where SEC filings, proxy materials, ESG and investor information, disclosures, governance documents and shareholder services are available, what is incorporated by reference, and how to request documents or monitor disclosures.

nodes.summary: Defines abbreviations and terms for Pfizer products, businesses, organizations, and agreements, including WRDM and WTO. Notes COVID-19 product emergency-use authorizations and limitations, cautions on interpreting clinical-study data, and explains rounding and trademark conventions. Describes where to access Pfizer SEC filings, proxy and ESG reports, investor and governance information, shareholder services, and required disclosures, including incorporation-by-reference exclusions and contact details.

nodes.summary: Pfizer cautions that forward-looking statements in its filings and public communications involve uncertainty, may differ materially from outcomes, speak only as of their date, and generally will not be updated; it identifies broad forecasts and specific expectations, then outlines non-exhaustive risks involving R&D and regulation, product safety and competition, acquisitions and operations, COVID-19 products, markets and macroeconomic conditions, government policy and litigation, intellectual property, IT and cybersecurity, and environmental goals. The text describes Pfizer’s global biopharmaceutical business, patient-focused purpose, value and access approach, six ESG priorities, growth strategy and 2022 acquisitions of Arena, GBT and Biohaven. It also explains its two-segment commercial structure—Biopharma and PC1—and organizational changes begun in 2022.

nodes.title: Pfizer Business, Strategy, and Key Risks
nodes.summary: The page notes risks from international minimum-tax rules and potential U.S. tax-law changes, as well as IT outages, cyberattacks, and intellectual-property disputes or limits. It describes Pfizer as a global research-based biopharmaceutical company, its products’ health and economic value, patient access and pricing efforts, purpose, and six ESG priorities. It outlines growth through its pipeline, existing products, and business development, including 2022 acquisitions of Arena, GBT, and Biohaven.

nodes.title: COMMERCIAL OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: Pfizer moved to a global structure in 2021 with Biopharma and PC1 (its contract development/manufacturing and specialty-API business). From Q3 2022, it reorganized Biopharma, R&D, and enabling/platform functions to leverage expertise, prioritize R&D, prepare for potential launches, and support three customer groups: Primary Care (former Internal Medicine and Vaccines portfolios, plus COVID-19 and potential mRNA/antiviral products); Specialty Care (former Inflammation & Immunology, Rare Disease, and most Hospital products); and Oncology (biologics, small molecules, immunotherapies, and biosimilars). The text lists representative products for each group and directs readers to Note 17 and MD&A for segment, product-revenue, and revenue-driver information, and to the Risk Factors—Concentration section for risks from reliance on major products.

nodes.title: RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
nodes.summary: R&D supports Pfizer’s mission by developing new therapies and improving existing products, with priorities spanning differentiated medicines and vaccines, long-term capabilities, and innovative partnerships. Work focuses on six therapeutic areas and combines internal research with external collaborations, licenses, acquisitions, and investments. Global operations use WRDM for research and early development and GPD for clinical development and regulatory work, coordinated by senior leaders to allocate resources across the portfolio. R&D spending is not reported by phase or area because resources can shift quickly. Drug development may take over ten years; pipeline projects and candidate information are discussed elsewhere, and development is costly, time-consuming, unpredictable, and subject to identified risks.

nodes.title: COLLABORATION AND CO-PROMOTION
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes collaborations and co-promotion arrangements supporting development, R&D, sales, and distribution. Comirnaty is jointly developed and commercialized with BioNTech, with equal development costs and gross-profit sharing worldwide except China, Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan, subject to local authorization. Eliquis is partnered with BMS, with shared development costs and profits or losses, subject to market-specific arrangements. Xtandi is partnered with Astellas, with shared U.S. profits, losses, and costs, plus tiered international royalties. Bavencio is partnered with Merck KGaA, with most costs and profits shared equally. Orgovyx and Myfembree are partnered with Myovant in specified markets, with shared profits and expenses; Myovant temporarily covers Pfizer’s eligible expenses up to $50 million for 2022 and leads regulatory, supply, and combination-tablet development responsibilities. Revenue is generally reported as Alliance revenues, except certain direct sales and most Comirnaty revenue. Pipeline collaborations include BioNTech’s shingles vaccine and Valneva’s Lyme disease vaccine candidate. The text points readers to related MD&A, risk-factor, and financial-statement-note disclosures.

nodes.title: INTERNATIONAL OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: Pfizer operates globally, supplying medicines and vaccines to over 185 countries and territories. Emerging markets are central to its growth strategy, with urbanization and a rising middle class creating opportunities. In 2022, international revenue was $57.9 billion, or 58% of total revenue; more than $500 million in revenue was generated in 24 countries, versus 21 in 2021 and 8 in 2020, largely due to Comirnaty and, in 2022, Paxlovid. Japan was the largest non-U.S. market by revenue share. The company directs readers to its geographic revenue disclosures and notes risks associated with international operations, including regulatory and pricing constraints.

nodes.title: SALES AND MARKETING
nodes.summary: The text describes Pfizer’s sales channels for prescription biopharmaceuticals and vaccines, including government contracts for Comirnaty and Paxlovid, their expected U.S. shift to commercial channels in late 2023, and the possibility that some government contracts may change or end. It covers efforts to secure formulary access and collaborate on disease-management programs; lawful promotion to healthcare providers, patients, insurers, employers and governments; consumer and public-health advertising; and hybrid in-person and virtual customer engagement, expanded during the pandemic.

nodes.title: PATENTS AND OTHER INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS
key_items: Major Europe Basic Product Patent Expiration Year (1)
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its patents covering products, uses, formulations and manufacturing, noting that duration, scope, extensions and remedies vary by country; weak IP protection can constrain operations, while regulatory exclusivity may overlap with patents. A product-by-product table lists estimated basic patent expirations in the U.S., Europe and Japan, with qualifications on extensions, exclusivity, collaborations, approvals and litigation. Loss or invalidation of rights, settlements, or expired licenses can trigger generic competition and sharply reduce revenue; Pfizer defends its rights, but exclusivity timelines are uncertain, and some products, including Sutent, have already lost protection. Trademarks and trade dress receive fixed renewable or use-based protection.

nodes.title: COMPETITION
nodes.summary: The text describes intense, regulated competition from branded and generic drugs, biosimilars, and alternative vaccines, based on efficacy, safety, convenience, and cost. Competitors’ R&D, patent challenges, and lower costs can erode sales or make products obsolete. The company counters through R&D, business development, post-approval research, education, ethical marketing, organizational improvements, and affordability/access programs. It seeks early biosimilar market entry. Generics benefit from lower costs, streamlined approval, payer and government preference, and substitution policies; competition may intensify in China. Biosimilars offer highly similar, lower-cost biologic alternatives and are approved under U.S. law.

nodes.title: PRICING PRESSURES AND MANAGED CARE ORGANIZATIONS
key_items: Commercial Pricing Pressures; Managed Care Organizations
nodes.summary: The text describes commercial pricing pressures from cost-conscious employers, payers, and provider purchasers, including higher patient costs, tougher negotiations, coverage limits, and discounts. It discusses the shift toward outcomes-based and risk-sharing payments, their potential effects on prices, access, utilization, and provider finances during and after COVID-19, and the company’s efforts to improve affordability, access, and evidence of product value. It also explains the growing influence and consolidation of U.S. managed care organizations and PBMs, their use of formularies, protocols, purchasing, and tiering to control costs, and how coverage restrictions affect drug use and competition; the company seeks formulary access as branded products increasingly face non-preferred status.

nodes.title: RAW MATERIALS
nodes.summary: The company sources essential raw materials from numerous global suppliers, generally in sufficient quantities and often from multiple sources. It anticipates no significant supply-related operational impact in 2023, but rising industry demand for some components and materials could constrain supply and affect future business. It is monitoring risks and mitigating them through supplier management, qualifying additional suppliers, and advance purchasing where possible.

nodes.title: GOVERNMENT REGULATION AND PRICE CONSTRAINTS
key_items: Drug and Biologic Regulation; Biosimilar Regulation; Sales and Marketing Regulations
New Drug Approvals; Pricing and Reimbursement
Healthcare Provider Transparency and Disclosures; Intellectual Property; Data Privacy
nodes.summary: The text surveys extensive global regulation affecting Pfizer, noting compliance costs and potential penalties, business, and reputational harm. In the U.S., it covers FDA and other agency oversight of drug development, approval, manufacturing, safety, promotion, supply chains and emergency authorizations; biosimilar exclusivity; fraud, marketing, anti-corruption and privacy rules; and pricing, reimbursement and access pressures, including Medicaid, 340B, the Inflation Reduction Act, state policies, and payer consolidation. Internationally, it reviews approval and pharmacovigilance systems, government pricing controls—especially China’s reimbursement negotiations and generic procurement—provider-payment transparency, intellectual-property protections and challenges, and evolving data-privacy laws.

nodes.title: ENVIRONMENTAL MATTERS
nodes.summary: Pfizer complies with environmental laws and is cleaning up contamination from past industrial activity. In 2022, it spent $88 million on environment-related capital expenditures and $148 million on other environmental expenses; it does not expect compliance costs to materially affect its financial position. Pfizer also set a 2040 net-zero goal under the Science Based Targets initiative, targeting 95% lower operational GHG emissions and 90% lower value-chain emissions versus 2019. Its reduction plan will include new technologies, climate solutions, and supplier action. 2022 related spending was not material; near-term financial effects are not expected to be material, though longer-term effects are uncertain. The filing refers readers to its climate and sustainability risk disclosures.

nodes.title: HUMAN CAPITAL
key_items: Diversity, Equity and Inclusion; Colleague Engagement; Performance, Leadership and Growth; Health, Safety and Well-Being; Pay Equity
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its workforce, inclusive workplace goals and four core values: Courage, Excellence, Equity and Joy. It outlines diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, colleague engagement surveys and 2022 engagement results, performance reviews, leadership and non-linear career development, and global health, safety and well-being programs, including COVID-19 measures and a flexible work model planned for 2023. It also states its commitment to role-based equitable pay and annual public pay-equity reporting.

Covers forward-looking-statement cautions and risks; Pfizer’s business, strategy, acquisitions, organization, commercial segments, R&D, collaborations, global operations, and sales and marketing. Also addresses intellectual property, competition, pricing and managed care, raw-material supply, global regulation and price constraints, environmental compliance and climate goals, and workforce, inclusion, development, safety, well-being, and pay equity.

title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS

nodes.title: RISKS RELATED TO OUR BUSINESS, INDUSTRY AND OPERATIONS:
MANAGED CARE TRENDS
nodes.summary: The section cautions that listed risks are not exhaustive and that general economic, geopolitical, weather, and disaster risks could materially harm operations, finances, results, cash flows, prospects, reputation, or credit ratings; it includes forward-looking statements. Managed-care risks include payer consolidation and stronger cost-control efforts, formularies and consumer preference for generics, specialty-drug cost containment, pricing and access tools such as exclusions, prior authorization, and step therapy, and resulting pressure on product pricing and formulary access. Related business arrangements face government scrutiny, changing fraud-and-abuse safe harbors, and evolving legal and regulatory guidance.

nodes.title: COMPETITIVE PRODUCTS
nodes.summary: The text describes competitive risks from new products, rivals’ advantages, pricing and efficacy differences, generics, patent challenges and at-risk launches, and biosimilar competition and uptake barriers; these could reduce sales. It also notes revenue concentration: ten products generated 82% of 2022 revenue, with Comirnaty and Paxlovid at 57%, exposing Pfizer to product, safety, regulatory, patent, demand, pricing, supply and post-pandemic risks. Customer concentration and wholesaler/pharmacy consolidation may cause collection problems and increase pricing pressure.

nodes.title: RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
nodes.summary: Ongoing business strength and growth require replenishing products through internal R&D and partnerships or other arrangements, including new products and uses that meet unmet needs and secure payer reimbursement. The company must balance current growth, future investment, and shareholder returns amid high development costs and regulatory demands. Early development decisions affect marketing and reimbursement, and trials may not achieve the right balance of speed and outcomes. Candidates can fail or lack approval; poor choices of indications, investments, technologies, markets, or licensing opportunities can reduce pipeline productivity. Even promising science may fail commercially due to competition, access, or reimbursement barriers. Novel gene therapies have especially uncertain development timelines, costs, approval prospects, and acceptance by patients and medical professionals.

nodes.title: GLOBAL OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes risks from global operations, including economic, political, regulatory, trade, public-health and climate disruptions; emerging-market instability and government pricing controls; and currency, inflation, interest-rate and investment exposure. It outlines potential trade restrictions’ effects on sales, costs, pensions, counterparties and credit reserves. Manufacturing and distribution may face regulatory, supply, quality, capacity, recall and disaster-related problems; facility noncompliance can trigger sanctions. Chantix recalls and industry-wide nitrosamine reviews may lead to further market actions. Reliance on collaborators and service providers creates execution, compliance, cyber, labor, supply and relationship risks, while expiring alliances may reduce revenue. Counterfeits threaten patient safety, trust and sales, especially through e-commerce; Pfizer invests in education, technology and monitoring to combat them.

nodes.title: Operational, Financial, and Partnership Risks
key_items: PRODUCT MANUFACTURING, SALES AND MARKETING RISKS
COLLABORATIONS AND OTHER RELATIONSHIPS WITH THIRD PARTIES
nodes.summary: The text describes exposure to foreign currency, inflation, interest-rate, borrowing, and employee-benefit risks, noting the international share of revenue and referring readers to financial disclosures. It outlines risks to manufacturing, supply, distribution, sales, and marketing from operational disruptions, regulatory noncompliance, and product quality issues, including Chantix nitrosamine recalls and potential further market actions. It also explains reliance on third-party collaborators and service providers, upfront transaction costs, disruption and compliance risks, potential impacts on product development and commercialization, and possible declines in alliance revenue when agreements end.

nodes.title: COUNTERFEIT PRODUCTS
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s reputation and popular medicines and vaccines attract counterfeiters, whose unregulated, unsanitary products threaten patient safety and could undermine trust and cause lost sales, recalls, and litigation. Counterfeit medicines are an industry-wide problem worsened by e-commerce, especially during COVID-19, when reduced access to legitimate pharmacies drove consumers toward deceptive online offers and scams. Counterfeiters target high-demand products; Pfizer has seen increased attempts involving its internal-medicine portfolio and COVID-19 treatments. Pfizer combats counterfeiting through education, detection technologies, supply monitoring and law-enforcement cooperation, and engagement with policymakers, but these efforts may not prevent the problem from growing.

The section outlines risks that could materially affect Pfizer’s operations, finances, results, cash flows, prospects, reputation, or credit ratings, including economic, geopolitical, weather, disaster, and forward-looking uncertainties. It covers managed-care cost controls, payer consolidation, generics, pricing and access restrictions, and regulatory scrutiny of business arrangements; competition from new products, generics, patent challenges, and biosimilars; and revenue and customer concentration. It describes R&D costs, candidate failures, approval, reimbursement, commercialization, and gene-therapy uncertainties. Global and operational risks include political, regulatory, trade, public-health, climate, currency, inflation, interest-rate, manufacturing, quality, supply, distribution, recall, compliance, and facility disruptions. It also addresses dependence on collaborators and service providers, alliance costs and expirations, and counterfeit medicines’ threats to safety, trust, and sales, alongside Pfizer’s mitigation efforts.

nodes.title: RISKS RELATED TO GOVERNMENT REGULATION AND LEGAL PROCEEDINGS:
key_items: PRICING AND REIMBURSEMENT; U.S. HEALTHCARE REGULATION
DEVELOPMENT, REGULATORY APPROVAL AND MARKETING OF PRODUCTS
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from global drug pricing controls, reimbursement reforms, U.S. healthcare regulation and spending cuts, and international payer and vaccine-tender decisions. Drug and vaccine development and approval are uncertain, costly, and vulnerable to trial failures, regulatory delays, changing interpretations, safety concerns, and adverse advisory recommendations. Post-approval studies and emerging safety data may prompt label changes, restrictions, or loss of approval; it details required monitoring for Xeljanz, Comirnaty, and Paxlovid. Legal risks include patent, product, commercial, securities, and other litigation; government investigations and penalties; marketing and pricing compliance; disclosure obligations; the company’s Corporate Integrity Agreement; and uncertain legal and environmental liabilities.

nodes.title: RISKS RELATED TO INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY, TECHNOLOGY AND SECURITY:
nodes.summary: The text describes risks to Pfizer’s intellectual property and technology security. Patent, trademark, trade dress, copyright, trade-secret, domain-name and contractual protections may be unavailable, inadequate, delayed, challenged or unenforceable across jurisdictions; policy changes, including potential compulsory licensing, could also limit protection. Generic and biosimilar challenges, at-risk launches, patent proceedings, damages claims, trademark disputes, loss of licenses, and unauthorized use or independent development could harm sales and finances. Pfizer may challenge others’ rights or pursue biosimilar opportunities, but litigation can delay launches, incur costs, or fail; infringement findings could lead to injunctions, royalties, damages or enhanced damages, including disputes involving Comirnaty, Paxlovid and mRNA products. IT and third-party systems face increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks, outages, supply-chain vulnerabilities and data breaches that could cause operational, financial, legal, regulatory and reputational harm; controls and cyber insurance may not prevent or fully cover losses.

summary: Identifies risks that could materially affect Pfizer’s business, financial results, cash flows, prospects, reputation, or credit ratings. Topics include market access, pricing, competition, R&D, approvals, commercialization, global operations, manufacturing and supply, collaborators, counterfeits, government regulation, product safety, litigation, investigations, and legal liabilities. It also covers intellectual-property disputes and technology, cybersecurity, and data risks; acquisitions and other transactions; COVID-19, climate and ESG matters; investment and benefit-plan volatility; costs, impairments, and changes in laws, taxes, and accounting standards.

title: ITEM 2. PROPERTIES
summary: The company owns and leases global facilities for commercial, operational, research, manufacturing, distribution and corporate functions, often co-located for efficiency. Its headquarters moved to The Spiral in New York’s Hudson Yards in February 2023; it had 301 properties totaling about 40 million square feet at year-end 2022. PGS leadership is based mainly in New York and Peapack, New Jersey, and oversees 36 plants and multiple distribution sites worldwide; it expected to exit its Perth site in early 2023. The company considers its properties suitable for current and foreseeable needs and refers to Note 9 for property and equipment investment amounts.

All are members of the Pfizer Executive Leadership Team and serve until successors are appointed at the 2023 annual meeting or earlier death, resignation, or removal. Officers covered are Albert Bourla, David Denton, Mikael Dolsten, Lidia Fonseca, Angela Hwang, Rady Johnson, Douglas Lankler, Aamir Malik, Michael McDermott, William Pao, Payal Sahni, and Sally Susman.

nodes.title: OVERVIEW OF OUR PERFORMANCE, OPERATING ENVIRONMENT, STRATEGY AND OUTLOOK
Pfizer Inc.
nodes.summary: Pfizer reports 2022 revenue of $100.3 billion, operating cash flow of $29.3 billion, reported diluted EPS of $5.47 and adjusted EPS of $6.58, with year-over-year changes; adjusted EPS is non-GAAP, and operational variances exclude foreign exchange. The company describes its global biopharmaceutical purpose, access commitments, growth strategy, 2023 investments, portfolio and organizational transformation, segments, Upjohn separation costs, and restructuring and R&D optimization. It highlights pipeline innovation, demographic and scientific growth opportunities, and business development through pipeline advancement, product optimization, portfolio reviews and strategic transactions.

nodes.title: Our 2022 Performance
nodes.summary: In 2022, revenue rose 23% to $100.3 billion, driven mainly by Paxlovid and Comirnaty; excluding these products, operational revenue grew 2%, with gains in several established and acquired products offset by declines in others. The company forecast 2023 revenue of $67–71 billion, a 31% operational decline at the midpoint, as lower COVID-19 product sales are partly offset by growth in its non-COVID portfolio, launches, and acquired products. Pretax income from continuing operations increased $10.4 billion to $34.7 billion, mainly on higher revenue and lower acquired R&D charges, partly offset by higher costs and expenses, equity-security losses, and lower pension credits. The text directs readers to related MD&A sections and notes for revenue drivers, COVID-19 expectations, product indications, income analysis, and tax information.

key_items: Intellectual Property Rights and Collaboration/Licensing Rights
Regulatory Environment/Pricing and Access––Government and Other Payer Group Pressures
nodes.summary: Pfizer outlines key operating challenges: costly, risky R&D and ongoing product safety monitoring; revenue exposure from patent and licensing expirations, with moderate expiry impacts in 2023–2025 and larger ones in 2026–2030; growing global pricing and access pressures, including U.S. reforms such as the IRA and possible Medicaid or 340B changes; recalls and potential supply constraints despite largely normal 2022 operations and mitigation efforts; and economic, political, geopolitical, public-health, and climate risks affecting global business. It also notes COVID-19 products Paxlovid and Comirnaty, including an Omicron-adapted booster.

nodes.title: Pfizer Inc.
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes ongoing Comirnaty and Paxlovid research, including variant-adapted vaccines, boosters, combination vaccines, next-generation treatments, and additional Paxlovid populations. It expects COVID-19 product sales to shift from government contracts toward commercial channels during 2023–24; forecasts 2023 revenues of $13.5 billion for Comirnaty and $8 billion for Paxlovid, with significant demand and market uncertainties. COVID-19 has affected healthcare activity and Pfizer’s business, and its future impact remains unpredictable. Regarding Russia’s war against Ukraine, Pfizer continues supplying medicines but has halted new trials, recruitment, and manufacturing investments in Russia, donated about $25 million to humanitarian relief, and warns that escalation or sanctions could harm operations and results, despite Russia and Ukraine representing under 1% of revenue and assets.

Pfizer reviews its 2022 financial and operating performance, revenue drivers, income changes, and 2023 outlook, including the expected decline in COVID-19 product sales and growth in its non-COVID portfolio. It describes its purpose, strategy, investments, organizational and portfolio changes, pipeline and business-development priorities, and operating challenges including R&D risks, patent expirations, pricing and access pressures, supply issues, and global uncertainties. It also covers COVID-19 research and commercial transitions, and the operational and humanitarian effects of Russia’s war against Ukraine.

It also identifies income-tax assets, liabilities, uncertain tax positions, and ordinary-course tax, legal, guarantee, and indemnification contingencies, with references to relevant notes and disclosures.

It also reports income-tax provisions and effective rates and refers readers to notes and prior filings for further detail on discontinued operations, patents, litigation, and accounting matters.

nodes.summary: Pfizer’s January 2023 pipeline update describes its research, development candidates, indications, phases, and mechanisms. The text lists COVID-19 vaccine approvals and filings by age group and region, plus regulatory milestones for other products across the U.S., EU, and Japan. It notes labeling and safety updates for Xeljanz/Cibinqo, Chinese approvals, and Paxlovid’s extended FDA review. It also identifies late-stage additional indications and new drug candidates, their proposed uses, and development partners.

Reviews 2022 performance, strategy, outlook, operating environment, risks, and the effects of COVID-19 and the Ukraine war; explains critical accounting estimates and contingencies; analyzes revenue, expenses, taxes, and other income-statement changes; and summarizes pipeline developments, product approvals, filings, safety updates, and candidate indications.

summary: Pfizer explains Adjusted income and Adjusted diluted EPS as non-GAAP measures management uses to assess recurring operations, forecast performance, and inform budgeting and compensation, while noting their limitations and that they do not replace comparable GAAP measures or other performance tools. It describes 2022 methodology changes and restated prior periods, including treatment of acquired IPR&D, intangible amortization, acquisition-related items, discontinued operations, and significant items. Reconciliation tables show GAAP-to-adjusted line items and results for 2020–2022, with explanatory notes on taxes, R&D, restructuring, legal, equity-method, and other adjustments.

title: ANALYSIS OF THE CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS
summary: The text reviews Pfizer’s 2022 cash flows from continuing operations and directs readers to the 2021 Form 10-K for 2021-versus-2020 drivers and 2020 discontinued-operations cash flows. Operating cash flow fell to $29.267 billion, mainly due to higher Comirnaty profit-split payments to BioNTech and Paxlovid inventory buildup, partly offset by higher adjusted net income and payment timing. Investing cash use fell to $15.783 billion, reflecting investment redemptions, lower short-term investment purchases, and a $4 billion JV dividend, partly offset by $23 billion in acquisitions. Financing cash use rose to $14.834 billion, driven mainly by $2 billion in share repurchases, higher debt repayments, and lower debt issuance. 2021 discontinued-operation cash flows primarily involved Meridian, Upjohn, and the Mylan-Japan collaboration.

title: ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION, LIQUIDITY, CAPITAL RESOURCES AND MARKET RISK
summary: Pfizer describes its liquidity, funding sources, cash management, credit ratings, and capital allocation, including dividends and 2022 share repurchases. It outlines off-balance-sheet arrangements, indemnities, contractual obligations, tax payments, commitments, capital spending, leases, and terminated GSK-related guarantees. It discusses hyperinflationary operations and foreign-exchange, interest-rate, and equity-price risks, plus the LIBOR-to-SOFR transition. It summarizes recently adopted and issued accounting standards, expected effects and effective dates, and incorporates the market-risk discussion for Item 7A.

title: Market Risk and New Accounting Standards
key_items: ITEM 7A. QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
summary: Discusses equity price risk from life-science investments, noting potential income volatility but insignificant modeled adverse effects, and LIBOR transition plans and expected immaterial impact. Summarizes recently adopted standards by reference and newly issued guidance on reference-rate reform, equity-security sale restrictions, and supplier-finance disclosures, including effective dates, adoption options, and expected financial-statement effects. Market-risk disclosures are incorporated by reference to the MD&A.

title: ITEM 8. FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENTARY DATA

nodes.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
key_items: Opinion on the Consolidated Financial Statements
Evaluation of the U.S. Medicare, Medicaid, and performance-based contract rebates accrual
Evaluation of gross unrecognized tax benefits
nodes.summary: The independent auditor gives an unqualified opinion that Pfizer’s 2020–2022 consolidated financial statements fairly present its financial position, results, and cash flows under U.S. GAAP, and reports effective internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2022. The report explains management’s and the auditor’s responsibilities and PCAOB audit procedures. It identifies two critical audit matters: estimating U.S. Medicare, Medicaid, and performance-based rebate accruals, assessed through control testing, independent estimates, and comparisons with historical payments; and evaluating $4.5 billion in gross unrecognized tax benefits, which requires complex judgment about tax law and audit outcomes.

nodes.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
key_items: Evaluation of product liabilliy and other product-related litigation; February 23, 2023
Evaluation of product liabilliy and other product-related litigation
nodes.summary: The auditor describes procedures for the critical audit matter involving uncertain tax positions: testing related controls and calculations, assessing tax-law interpretations and transfer pricing with specialists, and inspecting tax settlements and statute expirations. It also identifies product liability and related litigation as a critical audit matter because estimating losses involves substantial uncertainty, and describes procedures including control testing, reviewing counsel letters and Audit Committee minutes, comparing past estimates with outcomes, and analyzing public information. The firm notes it has audited Pfizer since at least 1942, and dates the report February 23, 2023, in New York.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statements of Income
nodes.summary: Pfizer Inc.’s consolidated income statement for 2022, 2021, and 2020 presents revenues; operating costs and expenses, including cost of sales, selling and administrative, research and development, acquired in-process research and development, intangible amortization, restructuring and acquisition-related costs, and other income or deductions; continuing-operations income and taxes; discontinued operations; net income and noncontrolling interests; basic and diluted earnings per share by continuing and discontinued operations; and weighted-average basic and diluted shares. Footnotes clarify amortization exclusions and refer to Note 1L; accompanying notes are cited.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s consolidated comprehensive income statement presents 2022, 2021 and 2020 results, including net income; foreign-currency translation, derivative, available-for-sale securities and benefit-plan adjustments; other comprehensive income before and after tax and noncontrolling interests; and comprehensive income attributable to Pfizer and noncontrolling interests. Footnotes identify where derivative and securities gains or losses were reclassified in income, and the statement refers to accompanying notes.

summary: Presents the independent auditor’s unqualified opinion on Pfizer’s 2020–2022 consolidated financial statements and effective internal controls, explaining audit responsibilities and procedures. It discusses critical audit matters involving rebate accruals, uncertain tax positions, and product liability litigation, including the auditor’s assessment procedures, and notes the firm’s tenure and report date. The section also provides consolidated income and comprehensive income statements for 2020–2022, covering revenues, expenses, continuing and discontinued operations, earnings per share, share counts, other comprehensive income components, and related footnotes.

title: Consolidated Balance Sheets
summary: Pfizer Inc.’s consolidated balance sheets as of December 31, 2022 and 2021 present assets, liabilities, and equity in millions (except per-share data). Assets include cash and investments, receivables, inventories, tax and other current assets, equity-method investments, property and equipment, intangible assets, goodwill, and other noncurrent assets. Liabilities include borrowings and debt, payables, taxes, compensation, deferred revenues, benefit obligations, and other liabilities. The statement also reports commitments and contingencies, preferred and common stock, paid-in capital, treasury stock, retained earnings, accumulated comprehensive loss, noncontrolling interests, and total liabilities and equity; accompanying notes apply.

title: Consolidated Statements of Equity
summary: Pfizer’s 2020–2022 consolidated statements of equity report changes in preferred and common stock, additional paid-in capital, treasury stock, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive loss, noncontrolling interests, and total equity, including earnings, dividends, share transactions, the Upjohn distribution, and related notes. Consolidated cash flow statements for 2020–2022 detail operating, investing, and financing cash flows, exchange-rate effects, and beginning and ending cash balances. Supplemental disclosures report cash paid or received for taxes, interest, and interest-rate hedges, plus lease right-of-use assets obtained for lease liabilities.

title: Note 1. Basis of Presentation and Significant Accounting Policies
key_items: A. Basis of Presentation; B. New Accounting Standard Adopted in 2022; C. Estimates and Assumptions
B. New Accounting Standard Adopted in 2022
summary: Pfizer’s consolidated statements follow U.S. GAAP, define consolidation and fiscal-year timing for U.S. and international subsidiaries, and eliminate intercompany transactions. The note describes its 2021–22 operating reorganizations and Biopharma as its sole reportable segment, divestitures and spin-offs presented as discontinued operations, related equity treatment, other transactions, and prior-period reclassifications and rounding. Pfizer early adopted a 2022 business-combination standard for acquired contract assets and liabilities prospectively with no impact. It also explains the broad use, uncertainty, review, and potential financial effects of estimates and assumptions.

title: Pfizer Inc.

nodes.title: Pfizer Inc. (intro)
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s notes describe its U.S. GAAP consolidated reporting, fiscal-year differences for foreign subsidiaries, segment reorganizations, discontinued businesses and prior-period reclassifications. They cover adoption of a 2022 contract-accounting standard with no financial impact; the use and uncertainty of estimates; acquisition accounting and contingent consideration; fair-value methods, input levels and valuation practices; foreign-currency translation; and revenue recognition when product control transfers, including bill-and-hold criteria.

nodes.title: Acquisitions, Fair Value, and Currency Translation
nodes.summary: Explains acquisition accounting, including fair-value recognition, transaction costs, goodwill, acquired IPR&D, and contingent consideration remeasurement. Describes fair-value measurement using exit prices, valuation approaches, input levels, techniques for financial instruments, and review of pricing services. Covers foreign-currency translation for international and highly inflationary operations, including exchange rates and where translation effects are recorded.

nodes.title: G. Revenues and Trade Accounts Receivable
key_items: Our Sales Contracts; Deductions from Revenues
nodes.summary: Pfizer explains revenue recognition upon transfer of product control, including bill-and-hold criteria, short-term sales contracts, and estimates for rebates, chargebacks, discounts, returns, and incentives. It describes customer and government/managed-care sales arrangements and related accrual methods, revenue concentration in major products, and intellectual-property expiry risks. It reports sales-related accrual balances and excludes sales taxes from revenue. Receivables are valued net of expected-credit-loss allowances using segmented pools and monitored risk factors. The text also covers accounting for collaboration revenues, costs, royalties, reimbursements, and milestones; inventory valuation and impairment; selling and advertising expenses; R&D expensing; and acquired in-process R&D payments before and after regulatory approval.

nodes.title: Revenue, Collaboration, and Expense Accounting Policies
key_items: I. Cost of Sales and Inventories
J. Selllng, Informational and Administrative Expenses; K. Research and Development Expenses; L. Acquired In-Process Research and Development Expenses
J. Selllng, Informational and Administrative Expenses
L. Acquired In-Process Research and Development Expenses
nodes.summary: The page explains that sales taxes collected for government are excluded from revenue and describes receivables’ net valuation, pooled expected-credit-loss estimates, monitoring, specific reserves, and write-offs. It outlines how collaboration receipts, payments, royalties, development reimbursements, and milestones are classified and recognized. Inventories use lower of cost or net realizable value, with impairment review and noncurrent classification when not expected to sell within 12 months. Selling and administrative costs, including advertising, and R&D costs are expensed as incurred. Pre-approval acquired IPR&D payments are expensed; post-approval milestones are capitalized and generally amortized, with separate reporting beginning in 2022.

nodes.title: Pfizer Inc.
key_items: M. Amortization of Intangible Assets, Depreciation and Certain Long-Lived Assets
N. Restructuring Charges and Other Costs Associated with Acquisitions and Cost-Reduction/Productivity Initiatives
O. Cash Equivalents and Statement of Cash Flows
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s accounting notes explain that customer sales taxes are excluded from revenue and describe receivables valuation, pooled expected-credit-loss estimates, monitoring, specific reserves, and write-offs. They outline accounting for collaboration revenues, costs, royalties, reimbursements, and milestone payments; inventory costing and impairment; selling and advertising expenses; R&D and acquired in-process R&D; depreciation, intangible assets, goodwill, and impairment testing; acquisition and productivity-related restructuring costs; and cash-equivalent definitions and cash-flow classifications for hedging instruments.

nodes.title: Pfizer Inc.
key_items: P. Investments and Derivative Financial Instruments
Q. Tax Assets and Liabilliies and Income Tax Contingencies
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s notes describe accounting policies for acquired collaboration and in-license costs; long-lived assets, depreciation, amortization, and impairment testing; acquisition- and productivity-related restructuring costs; cash equivalents and cash-flow classification; investments, equity-method accounting, and derivatives; and current/deferred tax assets and liabilities, valuation allowances, global intangible low-taxed income, cross-border tax benefits, repatriation taxes, and uncertain tax positions, including recognition, measurement, monitoring, and classification.

nodes.title: Pfizer Inc.
Pfizer Inc. (intro)
nodes.summary: The notes describe accounting policies for investments and derivatives, including valuation, impairment, gains and losses, equity-method accounting, and hedge reporting; current and deferred tax assets and liabilities, GILTI election, competent-authority tax benefits, repatriation taxes, and uncertain-tax-position recognition and measurement; pension and postretirement accounting and actuarial assumptions; legal and environmental contingency accruals and insurance recoveries; and share-based compensation. They also detail the 2022 GBT acquisition, its provisional purchase-price allocation and employee awards, and the Biohaven acquisition, retained spin-off interest, royalty arrangements, and related existing obligations.

nodes.title: Pension Plans, Contingencies, and Share-Based Payments
key_items: R. Pension and Postretirement Benefit Plans
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its defined benefit and contribution pension plans and retiree medical benefits, including immediate recognition of actuarial gains and losses, balance-sheet recognition of funded status, and the assumptions used to value obligations and plan assets. It explains accrual policies for probable, estimable legal and environmental losses and assured insurance recoveries, and fair-value accounting and expense recognition for share-based awards. The page also begins Note 2 on acquisitions, divestitures, investments, licensing, and collaborations.

nodes.title: A. Acquisitions
nodes.summary: Pfizer details acquisitions of GBT and Biohaven in October 2022, ReViral in June 2022, Arena in March 2022, Trillium in 2021, and Array in 2019, including purchase terms, products and pipelines, prior investments, spin-off and royalty arrangements, and contingent payments. It summarizes acquisition accounting: consideration and post-closing employee compensation, acquired intangible assets, goodwill, inventories, debt, deferred taxes, receivables and liabilities; provisional allocations for GBT, Biohaven and Arena; ReViral and Trillium treated as asset acquisitions with acquired IPR&D charges; and Array’s finalized allocation and 2020 measurement-period adjustments. Pro forma results were omitted because the acquisitions were not material.

nodes.title: B. Divestitures
key_items: Upjohn Separation and Combination with Mylan
nodes.summary: Reports Meridian’s December 2021 sale for $51 million cash and an after-tax loss of $167 million, plus post-sale service agreements and immaterial 2022 activity. Details the 2020 Upjohn spin-off and combination with Mylan to form Viatris, including the all-stock transaction, ownership split, $12 billion payment, financing and Pfizer debt repayments, accounting effects, separation costs, and transition agreements, balances, and cash flows. A table summarizes discontinued-operations results for 2020–2022; notes explain the periods’ components, including Meridian operations and EpiPen litigation, Upjohn and Mylan-Japan activities, debt interest and remeasurement, and post-close adjustments.

nodes.title: C. Equity-Method Investments
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its equity-method investments in Haleon/the Consumer Healthcare JV and ViiV. It details Haleon’s formation, 2022 demerger, Pfizer’s 32% ownership, carrying and fair values, currency translation, dividends, earnings recognized on a reporting lag, and amortization and separation-related adjustments to its initial $4.8 billion excess basis. Summarized investee financial information is provided. The text also covers the JV’s debt issuance, Pfizer’s limited indemnity of GSK’s guarantees, loans and dividends around the demerger, and repayment and termination of the indemnity. For ViiV, it explains Pfizer’s 11.7% stake, suspension of equity-method accounting after its carrying value reached zero, dividends recognized as income, and summarized financial information.

nodes.title: D. Licensing Arrangements
nodes.summary: The text describes Pfizer’s Valneva licensing arrangement for the VLA15 Lyme disease vaccine, covering six serotypes common in North America and Europe. Under the 2020 agreement, Valneva could receive up to $308 million: a $130 million upfront payment and $35 million in development milestones paid by 2022, plus $143 million in unpaid early-commercialization milestones. Valneva initially funded 30% of development costs; Pfizer led late-stage development and controlled commercialization in exchange for tiered royalties. In June 2022, Pfizer invested €90.5 million ($95 million) in Valneva and revised the terms: Valneva funds 40% of remaining shared development costs, royalties are 14%–22% rather than starting at 19%, and up to $100 million in sales-based milestones were added; other early-commercialization milestones were unchanged. Pfizer held a 6.9% Valneva stake at year-end 2022.

nodes.title: E. Collaborative Arrangements
key_items: Collaboration with Beam; Collaboration with Arvinas; Collaboration with Myovant
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its collaborative arrangements, including Biohaven (migraine medicines; later acquired), BioNTech (shingles and COVID-19 vaccines, shared costs/profits and geographic rights), Beam (gene-editing research), Arvinas (breast-cancer drug), Myovant (women’s health and prostate-cancer products), and CStone (China oncology). Terms include upfront and milestone payments, equity investments, royalties, licensing, and shared development or commercialization. The text also summarizes 2020–2022 collaboration revenues and expenses by financial-statement category, explains key year-over-year changes and classifications, and excludes other third-party transactions and costs.

nodes.title: A. Transforming to a More Focused Company Program
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s 2019 Consumer Healthcare JV and 2020 Upjohn spin-off reshaped it into a focused innovative medicines and vaccines company, prompting alignment of costs and support functions. The program reorganized corporate services, transformed commercial engagement and operations (including 2022 changes), optimized manufacturing, and, from late 2022, targeted R&D costs, cycle times, and portfolio priorities through digital tools, new clinical approaches, and external partnerships. Costs include severance, implementation, exits, transfers, and depreciation. R&D costs are estimated at $500 million, mainly cash and expected primarily through 2023. By year-end 2022, total program costs were $3.5 billion, including $1.4 billion for Biopharma; about 85% of expected costs had been incurred, with most remaining costs expected through 2023.

nodes.title: B. Key Activities
nodes.summary: The text presents Pfizer’s 2020–2022 acquisition and cost-reduction/productivity costs and credits, including restructuring charges (employee terminations, asset impairments and exit costs), transaction and integration costs, benefit credits, additional restructuring depreciation, implementation costs, and annual totals. Notes explain cost-reduction charges and acquisition-related expenses (Arena, GBT, Trillium and Array), asset-life changes, and implementation costs. It also outlines restructuring-accrual balances, provisions and utilization through 2022, foreign-currency adjustments, and current/noncurrent liability classifications.

Covers Pfizer’s accounting policies for investments, derivatives, taxes, pensions, contingencies, and share-based compensation; 2022 acquisitions and earlier acquisitions, divestitures, equity-method investments, licensing and collaboration arrangements; and the costs, accounting effects, and results of the Upjohn spin-off and other transactions. It also describes Pfizer’s transformation and restructuring programs, including their objectives, cost categories, 2020–2022 charges and credits, accrual balances, and expected remaining costs.

summary: Pfizer’s notes cover consolidated reporting, fiscal-year differences, segment changes, discontinued operations, reclassifications, and accounting-standard adoption. They explain estimates, acquisitions and contingent consideration, fair-value methods, currency translation, revenue recognition and related estimates, receivables and credit losses, collaborations, inventories, expenses, acquired R&D, fixed and intangible assets, goodwill, restructuring, cash flows, investments, derivatives, taxes, pensions, contingencies, and share-based compensation. They also discuss acquisitions, divestitures, licensing and equity-method arrangements, the Upjohn spin-off, and transformation programs, including costs, accruals, and expected remaining charges.

title: Note 4. Other (Income)/Deductions—Net
summary: The note details Pfizer’s 2020–2022 Other (income)/deductions—net components and employee termination, impairment and exit-cost amounts. Footnotes explain capitalized interest; equity-security investment gains/losses; collaboration, licensing and product-rights income; legal matters; impairments; JV equity-method results; and other income, including ViiV dividends, transition-service income and contingent-consideration changes. It describes major 2022 and 2020 intangible-asset impairments and their estimated fair values by asset type and hierarchy level. Impairments use fair-value estimates based on discounted projected cash flows, with assumptions for timing, competition, legal/regulatory risks, discount and tax rates.

title: Note 5. Tax Matters

nodes.title: A. Taxes on Income from Continuing Operations
nodes.summary: The note reports income from continuing operations before tax by U.S. and international location for 2020–2022, explaining annual changes through equity-security gains and losses, benefit credits, restructuring and acquisition costs, Paxlovid and Comirnaty income, R&D, and impairment charges. It details current and deferred U.S. federal, state/local, and international tax provisions or benefits. It explains effective-tax-rate changes in 2022 versus 2021 and 2021 versus 2020, including Consumer Healthcare JV initiatives, tax resolutions, earnings mix, and intangible-asset impairment benefits; acquired tax liabilities are excluded. Pfizer also describes installment payments through 2026 of its initial $15 billion repatriation tax, amounts due in 2023 and classified as current or noncurrent at year-end 2022, and possible variation from uncertain tax positions and tax-credit carryforwards.

nodes.title: B. Tax Rate Reconcillation
nodes.summary: The text reconciles Pfizer’s 2020–2022 U.S. statutory and effective tax rates, explaining the effects of foreign earnings and tax incentives, settlements, FDII, R&D credits, interest, and other items. It details deferred tax assets and liabilities by category and year, including drivers of 2022 changes such as acquisitions, pensions, R&D capitalization, carryforwards, and currency movements. It also describes available tax-loss and credit carryforwards, related limitations, and $60 billion of indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings for which no U.S. tax provision is recorded.

nodes.title: D. Tax Contingencies
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes uncertain tax positions, including net unrecognized tax benefits of $2.9 billion in 2022 and $4.5 billion in 2021, related tax assets, their balance-sheet classifications, and a 2020–2022 reconciliation of gross benefits and drivers. It reports interest and immaterial penalties, IRS and international audit status, and the possibility of up to a $100 million decrease in benefits within 12 months, with outcomes and timing uncertain. It also presents 2020–2022 tax provision or benefit components for other comprehensive income, noting no tax provision on certain indefinitely held foreign investments.

summary: Reports income before tax by geography, current and deferred tax provisions or benefits, effective-rate changes and their drivers, and installment payments of the repatriation tax. Reconciles statutory and effective tax rates; details deferred tax assets and liabilities, tax-loss and credit carryforwards and limitations, and foreign earnings indefinitely reinvested without U.S. tax provision. Describes uncertain tax positions, related benefits, assets, interest and penalties, audit status, potential changes, and tax effects in other comprehensive income.

title: Note 6. Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss, Excluding Noncontrolling Interests

nodes.title: Note 6. Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss, Excluding Noncontrolling Interests (intro)
nodes.summary: Note 6 presents 2020–2022 changes, net of tax, in accumulated other comprehensive loss by foreign-currency translation, derivatives, available-for-sale securities, benefit plans, and other prior-service items. It notes exclusions for noncontrolling interests, Haleon/Consumer Healthcare JV currency effects and net investment hedging, with a reference to the Upjohn distribution. Note 7 reports recurring fair-value measurements of financial assets and liabilities at December 31, 2022 and 2021, classified by Level 1 and Level 2, including investments, derivatives, and insurance contracts; footnotes describe restricted employee-benefit trusts and accounting for underlying assets.

nodes.title: Financial Assets and Liabilliies Not Measured at Fair Value on a Recurring Basis
nodes.summary: At December 31, 2022, long-term debt excluding the current portion had a $33 billion carrying value and a $30 billion estimated fair value, compared with $36 billion and $42 billion, respectively, in 2021; fair value used a market approach with Level 2 inputs. Differences between fair and carrying values for held-to-maturity debt securities, private equity securities, long-term receivables, and short-term borrowings were not significant in either year. Their fair values use Level 2 inputs for held-to-maturity debt securities and short-term borrowings, and Level 3 inputs for long-term receivables and private equity securities.

nodes.title: B. Investments
nodes.summary: The text details Pfizer’s short- and long-term investments and equity-method investments for 2022 and 2021, including classifications and life-sciences/private-equity and money-market footnotes. It reports debt-security holdings, fair values, unrealized gains and losses, maturity ranges, investment-grade diversification, and immaterial expected credit losses. It also summarizes realized and unrealized equity-security gains and losses, including adjustments and impairments. Short-term borrowings are tabulated for both years, with information on the $7 billion revolving credit facility, maturity dates, additional credit lines, and their largely unused status.

nodes.title: D. Long-Term Debt
nodes.summary: The text presents senior unsecured long-term debt by maturity and stated interest rates for 2022 and 2021, along with principal totals, fair-value and purchase-accounting adjustments, unamortized discounts and issuance costs, other debt, adjusted carrying amounts, and current portions. Debt is generally redeemable at varying prices plus accrued interest; 2023 notes were reclassified as current. It also reports 2020–2021 note issuances and 2020 repurchases, including a $36 million net loss on one retirement.

nodes.title: E. Derivative Financial Instruments and Hedging Activities
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes managing foreign-exchange risk with derivatives and foreign-currency debt, principally for euro, pound, yen, and Canadian-dollar exposures, including forecast intercompany inventory sales hedged up to two years and possible net-investment protection. It explains earnings and OCI accounting for fair-value, cash-flow, net-investment, and undesignated hedges, including excluded amounts. Interest-rate derivatives, mainly for U.S.-dollar fixed-rate debt, hedge fair-value changes or convert variable rates to fixed. Tables report derivative fair values and notionals for 2022 and 2021; inventory-sale hedge notionals were $4.4 billion and $4.8 billion, respectively.

summary: Presents 2020–2022 changes in accumulated other comprehensive loss, net of tax, by component, noting exclusions and specified currency-hedging effects. Also covers recurring and nonrecurring fair-value measurements; investments, debt securities, equity gains and losses, credit exposure, and short-term borrowings; long-term debt maturities, rates, adjustments, issuances and repurchases; and foreign-exchange and interest-rate derivatives, hedge accounting, fair values and notionals.

title: Pfizer Inc.
summary: Pfizer explains accounting for foreign-exchange fair value, cash-flow and net-investment hedges, non-designated contracts, and interest-rate derivatives, including how gains and losses flow through earnings or OCI. It presents 2021–2022 derivative notionals, fair values, hedge gains/losses, reclassifications, expected reclassification, hedge duration, and cumulative debt fair-value adjustments. The note also describes credit-risk monitoring for customers, investments and financial counterparties, investment safeguards and exposures, collateral arrangements, and related derivative balances.

title: Note 8. Other Financial Information
key_items: A. Inventories; B. Other Current Liabilliies
summary: Note 8 reports inventory components and balances: finished goods, work-in-process, and raw materials and supplies totaled $8.981 billion in 2022 and $9.059 billion in 2021; noncurrent inventory was $5.827 billion and $939 million, respectively. The decrease in current inventory mainly reflects lower Comirnaty stock, partly offset by acquired products and higher Paxlovid levels. Noncurrent inventory rose mainly from strategic Paxlovid stock-building; no recoverability issues are expected. Other current liabilities include amounts payable to BioNTech for Comirnaty’s gross-profit split: $5.2 billion in 2022 and $9.7 billion in 2021.

title: Note 9. Property, Plant and Equipment (PP&E)
key_items: Developed Technology Rights; IPR&D; Licensing Agreements
summary: Note 9 reports PP&E by asset type, useful life, accumulated depreciation and geographic area for 2022 and 2021. Note 10 details identifiable intangible assets by finite- and indefinite-lived category, gross and net carrying amounts, and accumulated amortization; changes primarily reflect acquisitions, amortization and an IPR&D impairment. It explains the nature and accounting treatment of developed technology rights, brands, IPR&D and licensing agreements, including approval, amortization and impairment rules; gives weighted-average useful lives, historical and forecast amortization; and reconciles goodwill changes, acquisition additions, foreign-exchange effects, and 2022 reallocation following organizational changes, with no impairment identified.

title: Note 11. Pension and Postretirement Benefit Plans and Defined Contribution Plans

nodes.title: A. Components of Net Periodic Benefit Costs and Changes in Other Comprehensive Income/(Loss)
nodes.summary: Note 11 describes employees’ eligibility for U.S. and international defined benefit and contribution retirement plans, including qualified and supplemental U.S. plans, plus retiree medical benefits. It reports 2020–2022 pension and postretirement benefit-cost components, comprehensive-income effects, and actuarial gain/loss drivers. It presents assumptions for plan costs and year-end obligations, explains annual reviews and discount-rate methods, notes higher 2022 obligation discount rates, and provides U.S. retiree healthcare trend assumptions for 2021–2022.

nodes.title: C. Obligations and Funded Status
nodes.summary: The notes detail Pfizer’s 2022 and 2021 pension and postretirement benefit-obligation and plan-asset changes, funded status and balance-sheet/accumulated-comprehensive-loss amounts, including actuarial effects, spin-off and settlement impacts, and plans with obligations exceeding assets. They present 2022/2021 asset allocations and fair-value hierarchy, Level 3 investment changes, valuation methods and assumptions, investment strategy and use of derivatives. They also disclose expected 2023 employer contributions and benefit payments through 2032, funding practices, and defined-contribution plan features and employer costs for 2020–2022.

nodes.title: Pension Cash Flows and Defined Contribution Plans
nodes.summary: Describes valuation methods for pension and postretirement plan assets across fair-value levels, NAV-based valuation of commingled and partnership investments, permitted derivatives, and investment objectives and allocation practices. Reports expected 2023 employer contributions and projected 2023–2032 benefit payments for U.S. and international plans, noting U.S. postretirement reimbursements exceed expected contributions. Summarizes U.S. and global defined contribution plans, employee contributions, employer matching, the U.S. and Puerto Rico Retirement Savings Contribution, and employer contribution charges of $770 million in 2022, $732 million in 2021, and $685 million in 2020.

summary: Covers employee eligibility and features of U.S. and international defined benefit and contribution plans, including supplemental pensions and retiree medical benefits. Reports 2020–2022 benefit costs, comprehensive-income and actuarial effects, plan assumptions, discount-rate methods and healthcare trends. Details 2021–2022 obligations, assets, funded status, balance-sheet amounts, actuarial, spin-off and settlement effects, asset allocations, fair-value levels and valuation methods, investment strategies and derivatives. Provides expected contributions and benefit payments through 2032, funding practices, and defined-contribution arrangements and employer costs.

title: Note 12. Equity
key_items: A. Common Stock Purchases; B. Preferred Stock and Employee Stock Ownership Plans
B. Preferred Stock and Employee Stock Ownership Plans
summary: Pfizer buys common shares through negotiated or open-market transactions; its board authorized a $10 billion repurchase program in December 2018, with purchases beginning in 2019. In first-quarter 2022, it repurchased 39 million shares for $2 billion, leaving about $3.3 billion authorized at year-end. Series A preferred stock held by an ESOP trust was converted into 1,070,369 common shares in May 2020; the preferred stock was eliminated from the corporate charter later that year. The Common ESOP’s shares were fully allocated to U.S. defined-contribution plan participants at December 31, 2022; related compensation cost was $19 million in each of 2020–2022.

title: Note 13. Share-Based Payments
summary: Notes 13–14 describe Pfizer’s share-based compensation programs, the 2019 Plan’s share authorization and limits, award types (TSRUs, RSUs, PPSs, PSAs, BPAs and options), eligibility, terms, valuation, vesting, settlement and expense recognition. They report award activity and outstanding balances, valuation assumptions, compensation expense and tax benefits for 2020–2022, plus TSRU/PTU conversions and option activity. The EPS note presents 2020–2022 basic and diluted income numerators, weighted-average share denominators and anti-dilutive equivalents, and explains ESOP share treatment.

title: Note 15. Leases
summary: Pfizer leases real estate, fleet and equipment, typically for 1–30 years, with some extension or termination options; reasonably certain extensions are included in lease terms. Some fleet leases have residual guarantees, and leases may include variable payments and taxes or other non-lease costs. Variable lease payments were $536 million, $381 million and $380 million in 2022, 2021 and 2020; Pfizer elected not to separate non-lease components. The note explains lease identification, classification, ROU assets and liabilities, and use of incremental borrowing rates. It reports balance-sheet classifications and lease-cost components, weighted-average lease terms and discount rates, cash paid and sale-leaseback gains or losses, and a 2022 maturity reconciliation from $3.844 billion of undiscounted payments to $3.217 billion present value, including current and noncurrent portions.

title: Note 16. Contingencies and Certain Commitments
key_items: B. Guarantees and Indemnifications; C. Certain Commitments; D. Contingent Consideration for Acquisitions
summary: Pfizer describes ordinary-course contingencies and commitments, including legal, tax, guarantees and indemnifications. It outlines legal risks, accounting uncertainty and loss accruals, then details patent disputes (including generic challenges and Comirnaty claims), product litigation, commercial, environmental and securities matters, and government investigations. It also summarizes transaction-related indemnities and guarantees, $4.4 billion in binding commitments, and contingent acquisition consideration of $645 million at year-end 2022, compared with $697 million in 2021.

nodes.title: Modification of Indenture
nodes.summary: A supplemental indenture may generally modify noteholders’ rights with consent from holders of a majority of the outstanding principal amount of all affected series, voting together. Each holder’s consent is required for changes to maturity, principal or interest payments, payment currency, enforcement rights at maturity, conversion rights, consent thresholds, or provisions governing waivers of past defaults or certain covenants.

nodes.title: Events of Default
nodes.summary: Events of Default include missed principal or premium payments, sinking fund or interest payments remaining unpaid for 60 days, uncured covenant breaches after 90 days’ written notice, and specified bankruptcy or insolvency actions. Defaults on other debt or another note series are not automatically defaults; the trustee may withhold nonpayment-default notices when it deems that best for holders. For a continuing default, the trustee or holders of at least 33% of a series may accelerate its principal and accrued interest. A majority may rescind acceleration before judgment if overdue amounts are paid and other defaults are cured or waived. A majority of affected series may waive defaults, except payment defaults and provisions requiring each holder’s consent to change. Trustee action generally requires reasonable indemnity; a series majority may direct proceedings or remedies subject to limits. The company must annually certify to the trustee whether defaults exist and describe them.

nodes.title: Defeasance
nodes.summary: Defeasance means discharge from some or all obligations under the indenture. Subject to additional conditions, the issuer may irrevocably deposit enough cash or government securities with the trustee to cover a series’ principal, interest, premiums, and other amounts through maturity or redemption. The issuer may then be fully discharged from obligations for that series or released from specified restrictive covenants and certain defaults. Exercising this option requires an officer’s certificate and an opinion of counsel confirming compliance with all conditions precedent.

nodes.title: SECTION 1. PURPOSE
nodes.summary: The Pfizer Inc. Global Performance Plan, amended and restated effective January 1, 2022, aims to foster a culture of high performance and attract, motivate, and engage committed colleagues who help achieve the Company’s annual financial, strategic, and operational goals.

nodes.title: SECTION 2. DEFINITIONS
nodes.summary: Defines the Plan’s key terms, including Company and governance roles; Affiliates, Employees, Participants, Awards, incentive pools, targets and opportunities; performance periods and eligible earnings, with country-specific calculations and exclusions; employment warnings, Cause, termination categories, retirement and separation; and tax, securities, executive-team, country-group and long-term incentive references. It also specifies relevant eligibility rules and grants designated executives or the Committee discretion over determinations.

nodes.title: SECTION 3. ADMINISTRATION
nodes.summary: The Compensation Committee, or designated executives and other delegates, administers the Plan and may set rules and Award terms, interpret provisions, select participants, determine targets, goals and awards, make related findings, and take or delegate necessary actions. It exercises discretion in the Company’s best interest, without fiduciary status or a requirement for uniform treatment; its decisions are final and binding, subject to law. The Committee may adjust awards or pool funding for extraordinary events or legal, regulatory, judicial or accounting changes; remedy Plan or Award defects, omissions or inconsistencies; and adjust awards or pool funding when assuming benefits in an acquisition or business combination.

nodes.title: SECTION 4. ELIGIBILITY
nodes.summary: Employees may participate only if designated by the Committee, generally not until the January 1 after a post-October 1 hire; they cannot join another annual cash incentive plan for the same period. U.S./Puerto Rico participants receiving compliance warnings are capped at 90% of the lesser of target or pre-individual-performance award; IFW recipients are capped at 75%. Awards depend on Committee-set funding tied to company goals, allocation by business unit, and individual performance. Target awards use specified earnings, percentage, amount, eligibility-period, country-group, and ELTI rules. Final awards are capped at 250% of target and may be adjusted for employment or organizational changes or legal requirements.

nodes.title: SECTION 6. PAYMENT OF AWARDS
nodes.summary: Awards are generally paid in a lump sum by the 15th day of the third month after the Performance Period ends, subject to local law or payroll schedules. Alternatively, they may be deferred under Committee procedures and Section 409A. Payments may be delayed if reasonably expected to violate securities or other laws, until payment can be made lawfully, and after involuntary termination until any required release is received.

nodes.title: SECTION 7. SPECIAL PAYMENT EVENTS
nodes.summary: Section 7 sets award treatment for special events: voluntary termination before a performance period ends forfeits the award; afterward, eligibility is at Committee discretion. Involuntary termination before period-end generally earns a prorated award based on eligible days and earnings/targets, subject to release and payment deadlines; post-2022 proration excludes nonworking notice days except for WARN terminations. Post-period termination remains eligible under plan rules; retirement-eligible involuntary terminations may be prorated. Cause or performance-related termination before period-end forfeits awards except where law requires; afterward, payment is discretionary. Retirement during the period may yield a discretionary prorated award, with exceptional adjustments based on forecasts and funding; retirement afterward follows active-participant rules. Eligible STD or paid leave participants with 90 eligible-earnings days receive prorated awards, excluding leave time, subject to performance and Company discretion; military differential pay includes an active-employee award calculation. Death during the period may result in a discretionary prorated award to the estate, payable by December 31 of the following year.

nodes.title: SECTION 8. AMENDMENT AND TERMINATION
nodes.summary: The Company may amend or terminate the Plan at any time, with or without notice, including after the performance period but before payment, and may change eligibility, funding, measures, targets, results, and terms to address local laws or customs. Payments remain subject to applicable government rules. The Committee may delegate authority to make legally required award changes or establish country sub-plans, and its designated officers may make non-substantive administrative changes. The Committee or designee may also amend awards prospectively or retroactively, without participant consent, to remedy potential Section 409A defects.

nodes.title: SECTION 9. DEFERRAL OF AWARDS UNDER THE COMPANY’S DEFERRED COMPENSATION PLAN
nodes.summary: The Committee may permit award deferrals under Pfizer’s Deferred Compensation Plan, subject to its terms and Section 409A. U.S. awards are taxable when paid, with withholding authorized; non-U.S. taxation follows local rules. The Plan aims to comply with Section 409A, permits award amendments to address defects, and gives no tax-outcome guarantees. Awards may be recouped after significant financial restatements and offset against certain employee debts. Awards are discretionary, non-guaranteed, and create no employment or continued-service rights; provisions may be severed or conformed to law, with flexibility for foreign participants and approved leaves. New York law governs, subject to controlling federal law.

Awards are variable, discretionary, and do not create employment rights; provisions address termination, consideration, severability, foreign participants, and approved leaves.
